opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a really interesting thread connecting these two phenomena, and it's one of the things that drew me to studying forgetting in the first place.

With grokking, you see a network that first fits the training data, essentially memorizes it, and test performance stays near chance for a long time. Then, often much later in training, it suddenly generalizes. A common interpretation is that the network first finds a solution that's easy to reach but doesn't capture the underlying structure. Then, through something like weight decay or other implicit pressures, it's slowly pushed away from that memorizing solution toward a simpler one that captures the actual rule.

What struck me is that the pressure there is really a kind of gradual forgetting. Weight decay is constantly eroding whatever the network has learned, and only the parts the data keeps reinforcing survive. Over time, the idiosyncratic, example-specific information gets worn away, and what remains is more general.

In our work on forgetting and relearning, we made that process explicit and more aggressive. Instead of relying on slow decay, you periodically perturb or reset parts of the network, say the later layers or some subset of weights, and then retrain. The idea is that each forgetting step disproportionately removes information that's fragile or hard to relearn, like memorized details of particular examples. The information that's easy to relearn tends to be the general, shared structure in the data. So repeated forget-and-relearn cycles act like a filter that favors features which are consistently useful.

So I see them as two points on a spectrum. Grokking is what happens when forgetting is slow and implicit, which is why generalization is so delayed. Iterative forgetting and relearning compresses that timeline by applying the pressure deliberately. In both cases, generalization emerges not just from learning more, but from selectively losing the things that don't deserve to be kept.

I think that framing is useful because we usually treat forgetting as purely bad, something to minimize, as in the continual learning literature. But in the right form, forgetting may be an essential ingredient of learning well. It also echoes ideas from cognitive science, where forgetting is sometimes viewed as adaptive, helping us abstract away from specifics.

r001.rationale: It describes training-fit memorization followed by movement toward a simpler solution that captures the rule under weight decay or other implicit pressures.

r002.rationale: It says weight decay erodes learned information, but does not state that weight decay becomes the primary driver of weight changes once training loss is low.

r003.rationale: It connects grokking’s shift toward general structure with forgetting example-specific information that is worn away while the data keeps reinforcing what is useful.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says iterative forgetting and relearning compresses the timeline relative to slow, implicit grokking.

r005.rationale: It presents grokking and forget-and-relearn as two points on the same spectrum and says both generalize through selective forgetting; it does not distinguish the intervention’s acceleration from evidence that normal training uses that mechanism.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of these as two windows onto the same underlying tension in how networks learn, which is the competition between a fast, cheap solution and a slow, structured one.

In grokking, the network first memorizes. It finds a high-norm, lookup-table-like solution that fits the training data almost immediately, and validation accuracy sits at chance for a very long time. Then, often after thousands of epochs of apparently nothing happening, generalization snaps into place. What's actually going on underneath is that the memorizing circuit and the generalizing circuit are both being built, but the generalizing one grows slowly. Weight decay, or any implicit pressure toward simpler, lower-norm solutions, gradually erodes the memorization and the structured circuit takes over. The "delay" is the time it takes for that handoff to complete.

Forgetting and relearning is the same dynamic viewed from the other side. If you train a network, then perturb it, reset a subset of weights, or switch to a new distribution and come back, the network often recovers the old task much faster than it learned it originally. That tells you the knowledge wasn't really destroyed. The expensive part of learning, finding the right representational structure, is still latent in the weights. What got forgotten is a thin, easily rebuilt layer on top. So forgetting is often a surface-level phenomenon, and relearning speed is a measure of how much deep structure survived.

The connection I find most compelling is that both phenomena separate two kinds of knowledge that loss curves lump together. There is the brittle, high-capacity fit to specific examples, and there is the compressed, reusable structure that actually generalizes. Grokking shows the second kind can be present and growing while the metrics look flat. Relearning shows the second kind can persist while the metrics look like the knowledge is gone. In both cases, accuracy is a lagging and misleading indicator of what the network knows.

There's also a practical thread. Interventions that speed up grokking, like stronger regularization or periodically resetting late layers, are essentially induced forgetting. You deliberately wipe the memorization layer so the generalizing circuit faces less competition. So forgetting isn't just a failure mode to avoid. Done selectively, it's one of the mechanisms by which generalization emerges at all.

r001.rationale: The response describes the generalizing circuit gradually taking over under pressure toward simpler solutions, but does not clearly state that continued training after perfect training accuracy moves among training-fitting solutions toward the training procedure’s inductive bias.

r002.rationale: It says weight decay gradually erodes memorization, but does not say that weight decay becomes the primary driver of weight changes once training loss is low.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts memorization with reusable structure, but does not connect simplification during grokking to forgetting information unnecessary for fitting the training set.

r004.rationale: It says interventions such as periodically resetting late layers speed up grokking by wiping the memorization layer, describing a forget-and-relearn style intervention that accelerates grokking.

r005.rationale: The response presents induced forgetting as a mechanism by which generalization emerges, but does not distinguish intervention-induced acceleration from evidence that normal training uses the same mechanism.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful connection is that getting an example right doesn’t necessarily mean the network has learned a stable, generalizable way to solve it. During training, an example can be learned, forgotten, and then learned again as the model’s representations change. So accuracy alone can hide quite a lot of what’s happening underneath.

Grokking makes that distinction particularly striking: the network can fit the training data long before it performs well on held-out examples. One possible interpretation is that it initially relies on memorization, while a more general solution develops more slowly and eventually becomes dominant. From that perspective, forgetting and relearning could reflect the model moving between different ways of solving the task.

But I’d be careful about treating those as the same phenomenon. Delayed generalization doesn’t require a visible drop in training accuracy. The model could change how it solves the training examples while continuing to get them right. So the connection I’d want to investigate is whether the underlying representations and mechanisms change in similar ways, rather than assuming that grokking is simply forgetting followed by relearning.

r001.rationale: The response says the model may shift between ways of solving the task, but does not state that continued training after perfect training accuracy moves it toward the training procedure’s inductive bias.

r002.rationale: It does not mention weight decay or explain its role in changing weights when training loss is low.

r003.rationale: It contrasts memorization with a general solution, but does not connect network simplification to forgetting information unnecessary for fitting the training set.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe a forget-and-relearn procedure or say it accelerates grokking.

r005.rationale: It cautions against equating grokking with forgetting and relearning, but does not distinguish accelerated grokking under an intervention from evidence about the mechanism of normal training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one useful way to connect them is to separate getting the training examples right from learning a solution that generalizes. In grokking, those can happen at very different times: the network fits the training data, but its internal solution continues to change before we see an improvement on held-out examples.

Forgetting and relearning raise a similar question about what’s happening underneath the measured performance. If a network stops performing well on a task, has it actually lost the useful representations, or has it just lost the ability to use them? If it learns the task much faster the second time, that suggests some useful structure survived.

So the connection, to me, is that accuracy doesn’t give you a complete picture of what the network has learned. You can have structure developing before generalization becomes visible, and you can have structure remaining after performance has disappeared. That doesn’t necessarily mean grokking and forgetting have the same mechanism, but it makes studying the trajectory of learning—and not just the final accuracy—really important.

r001.rationale: The response says the internal solution can continue changing after fitting the training data, but does not say it moves among training-fitting solutions toward the training procedure’s inductive bias.

r002.rationale: It does not mention weight decay or explain what drives weight changes once training loss is low.

r003.rationale: It discusses structure surviving forgetting, but does not connect grokking-related simplification to forgetting information unnecessary for fitting the training set.

r004.rationale: It does not state that a forget-and-relearn procedure accelerates grokking.

r005.rationale: It says grokking and forgetting may not share a mechanism, but does not distinguish accelerated grokking under a forget-and-relearn intervention from evidence about normal training.
